<a id="T050"></a>
## T050

- Date: 2001-09-11
- Place: New York, Washington D.C. and Pennsylvania, United States
- Region: North America
- Theme: studies and evaluations
- Status: `we-have-a-record`

Hijacked aircraft struck the World Trade Center and the Pentagon and crashed in Pennsylvania; the attacks are examined in the 9/11 Commission Report.

Summary: On 11 September 2001, hijacked aircraft struck the World Trade Center and the Pentagon and crashed in Pennsylvania. The attacks are examined in the 9/11 Commission Report (T077), and the FBI calls its investigation its largest case ever. Later the same month, the UN Security Council adopted resolutions 1368 and 1373 (T051, T055) and NATO issued its Article 5 statement (T052).

Citations:

- [US-911COMM](../sources/regions/north-america.md#US-911COMM) ([https://www.9-11commission.gov/report/](https://www.9-11commission.gov/report/))
- [FBI-911](../sources/regions/north-america.md#FBI-911) ([https://www.fbi.gov/history/famous-cases/911-investigation](https://www.fbi.gov/history/famous-cases/911-investigation))

<a id="T051"></a>
## T051

- Date: 2001-09-12
- Place: New York, United States (UN Security Council)
- Region: Global/UN
- Theme: UN and international frameworks
- Status: `we-have-a-record`

The UN Security Council adopted resolution 1368 (2001) condemning the 11 September attacks.

Summary: On 12 September 2001, the day after the 11 September attacks, the UN Security Council adopted resolution 1368. The Council said it was determined to combat by all means threats to international peace and security caused by terrorist acts, and its preamble recognizes the inherent right of individual or collective self-defence under the Charter.

Citation: [UNSC1368](../sources/regions/global-un.md#UNSC1368) ([https://undocs.org/S/RES/1368\(2001\)](https://undocs.org/S/RES/1368(2001)))

<a id="T052"></a>
## T052

- Date: 2001-09-12
- Place: Brussels, Belgium (NATO)
- Region: Europe
- Theme: UN and international frameworks
- Status: `we-have-a-record`

The North Atlantic Council stated that, if the attack was directed from abroad, it would be regarded as an action covered by Article 5 of the Washington Treaty.

Summary: On 12 September 2001, the North Atlantic Council stated that, if the attack on the United States was directed from abroad, it would be regarded as an action covered by Article 5 of the Washington Treaty (collective defence). NATO's own page says this is the first and only time Article 5 has been invoked.

Citations:

- [NATO-PR2001-124](../sources/regions/europe.md#NATO-PR2001-124) ([https://www.nato.int/cps/en/natohq/official_texts_18553.htm](https://www.nato.int/cps/en/natohq/official_texts_18553.htm))
- [NATO-ART5](../sources/regions/europe.md#NATO-ART5) ([https://www.nato.int/cps/en/natohq/topics_110496.htm](https://www.nato.int/cps/en/natohq/topics_110496.htm))

<a id="T053"></a>
## T053

- Date: 2001-09-18
- Place: Washington, D.C., United States
- Region: North America
- Theme: laws and treaties
- Status: `we-have-a-record`

The Authorization for Use of Military Force (Pub. L. 107-40) was enacted.

Summary: On 18 September 2001, the Authorization for Use of Military Force (Pub. L. 107-40) was enacted. It authorizes the President to use all necessary and appropriate force against those he determines planned, authorized, committed or aided the 11 September attacks, or harbored them. Its continued application was later examined by the Congressional Research Service (CRS-R43983, unconfirmed copy).

Citation: [US-AUMF2001](../sources/regions/north-america.md#US-AUMF2001) ([https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/PLAW-107publ40/pdf/PLAW-107publ40.pdf](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/PLAW-107publ40/pdf/PLAW-107publ40.pdf))

## T054

- Date: 2001-09-23
- Place: Washington, D.C., United States
- Region: North America
- Theme: laws and treaties
- Status: `we-have-a-record`

Executive Order 13224 on blocking property of designated persons was issued.

Summary: On 23 September 2001, Executive Order 13224 on blocking property of designated persons was issued. The order states its objectives include preventing terrorism and denying financing and financial services to terrorists and terrorist organizations.

Citation: [US-EO13224](../sources/regions/north-america.md#US-EO13224) ([https://www.state.gov/executive-order-13224/](https://www.state.gov/executive-order-13224/))

<a id="T055"></a>
## T055

- Date: 2001-09-28
- Place: New York, United States (UN Security Council)
- Region: Global/UN
- Theme: UN and international frameworks
- Status: `we-have-a-record`

The UN Security Council adopted resolution 1373 (2001), which established the Counter-Terrorism Committee.

Summary: On 28 September 2001, the UN Security Council adopted resolution 1373, which established the Counter-Terrorism Committee. It requires all States to prevent and suppress terrorist financing, criminalize providing funds for terrorist acts, and deny support to those involved. The Committee's executive arm, CTED, was created in 2004 (T073).

Citations:

- [UNSC1373](../sources/regions/global-un.md#UNSC1373) ([https://undocs.org/S/RES/1373\(2001\)](https://undocs.org/S/RES/1373(2001)))

- Date: 2001-10-26
- Place: Washington, D.C., United States
- Region: North America
- Theme: laws and treaties
- Status: `we-have-a-record`

The USA PATRIOT Act (Pub. L. 107-56) was enacted.

Summary: On 26 October 2001, the USA PATRIOT Act (Pub. L. 107-56) was enacted. Its long title says it is meant to deter and punish terrorist acts and enhance law enforcement investigatory tools. Some of its powers were later reviewed by the Justice Department Inspector General (T094) and the Privacy and Civil Liberties Oversight Board (T109), and the USA FREEDOM Act reformed them in 2015 (T115).

Citation: [US-PATRIOT2001](../sources/regions/north-america.md#US-PATRIOT2001) ([https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/PLAW-107publ56/pdf/PLAW-107publ56.pdf](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/PLAW-107publ56/pdf/PLAW-107publ56.pdf))

- Place: Washington, D.C., United States
- Region: North America

- Status: `we-have-a-record`

The US President issued a Military Order on detention, treatment and trial of certain non-citizens.

Summary: On 13 November 2001, the US President issued a Military Order on the detention, treatment and trial of certain non-citizens, which created military commissions. ## T059

- Date: 2001-12-14
- Place: London, United Kingdom
- Region: Europe
- Theme: laws and treaties
- Status: `we-have-a-record`

The UK Parliament enacted the Anti-terrorism, Crime and Security Act 2001, including detention powers in Part 4.

Summary: On 14 December 2001, the UK Parliament enacted the Anti-terrorism, Crime and Security Act 2001. Part 4 allowed suspected international terrorists who were not UK nationals to be certified and detained. Those detention powers were later found incompatible with the European Convention on Human Rights by the House of Lords (T080) and the European Court of Human Rights (T099).

Citation: [UK-ATCSA2001](../sources/regions/europe.md#UK-ATCSA2001) ([https://www.legislation.gov.uk/ukpga/2001/24/contents](https://www.legislation.gov.uk/ukpga/2001/24/contents))

- Date: 2004-03-11
- Place: New York, United States (UN Security Council)
- Region: Europe
- Theme: UN and international frameworks
- Status: `we-have-a-record`

The UN Security Council adopted resolution 1530 (2004) condemning the Madrid train bombings; the resolution's text attributed them to ETA (see NOTES.md on this attribution).

Summary: On 11 March 2004, the day of the Madrid train bombings, the UN Security Council adopted resolution 1530 condemning them; the resolution's text attributed the bombings to ETA. A 2008 UN Special Rapporteur report instead describes them as carried out by members of an international terrorist cell, which is recorded as the people-disagree milestone T150. This row records only what the resolution says.

- Notes: Second source on attribution: SR-ESP-2008 (A/HRC/10/3/Add.2) describes the 11 March 2004 bombings as 'carried out by members of an international terrorist cell', while UNSC1530 attributed them to ETA. Recorded as a people-disagree row in timeline-add.csv.

Citation: [UNSC1530](../sources/regions/europe.md#UNSC1530) ([https://undocs.org/S/RES/1530\(2004\)](https://undocs.org/S/RES/1530(2004)))

## T073

- Date: 2004-03-26
- Place: New York, United States (UN Security Council)
- Region: Global/UN
- Theme: UN and international frameworks
- Status: `we-have-a-record`

The UN Security Council adopted resolution 1535 (2004), establishing the Counter-Terrorism Committee Executive Directorate.

Summary: On 26 March 2004, the UN Security Council adopted resolution 1535, establishing the Counter-Terrorism Committee Executive Directorate (CTED). The resolution revitalized the Counter-Terrorism Committee created by resolution 1373 (T055), with CTED headed by an Executive Director. Its mandate was later renewed, for example by resolution 2617 (T131).

Citation: [UNSC1535](../sources/regions/global-un.md#UNSC1535) ([https://undocs.org/S/RES/1535\(2004\)](https://undocs.org/S/RES/1535(2004)))

- Region: Global/UN
- Theme: UN and international frameworks

The UN Security Council adopted resolution 1540 (2004) on non-state actors and weapons of mass destruction.

Summary: On 28 April 2004, the UN Security Council adopted resolution 1540 under Chapter VII of the Charter on non-State actors and weapons of mass destruction. It requires all States to refrain from supporting non-State actors seeking nuclear, chemical or biological weapons, and the 1540 Committee was set up to follow its implementation.

The US Supreme Court decided R. v. Bush, 542 U.S. 466 (2004), on federal court jurisdiction over habeas petitions from Guantanamo detainees.

Summary: On 28 June 2004, the US Supreme Court decided R. v. Bush, 542 U.S. 466, on whether federal courts had jurisdiction over habeas petitions from Guantanamo detainees. It is the first of the Guantanamo detention cases recorded in CTA6 (see also T090 and T096); according to the syllabus, the Court held that US courts have jurisdiction to consider challenges to the legality of the detention of foreign nationals captured abroad in connection with hostilities and held at Guantanamo Bay.

The US Supreme Court decided H. v. Rumsfeld, 542 U.S. 507 (2004), on due process for a US citizen detained as an enemy combatant.

<a id="T079"></a>
## T079

- Date: 2004-10-08
- Place: Global
- Region: Global/UN
- Theme: UN and international frameworks
- Status: `people-disagree`

Definitions differ: Security Council resolution 1566 (2004) describes terrorist acts in its own wording, while the 1937 League of Nations convention used a different definition.

Summary: This row records two different definitions. Security Council resolution 1566 (8 October 2004) describes terrorist acts as criminal acts, including against civilians, committed with intent to cause death or serious injury or to take hostages, to provoke terror, intimidate a population or compel a government or international organization (UNSC1566). The 1937 League of Nations convention instead required parties to criminalize listed acts, such as wilful acts causing death, grievous bodily harm or loss of liberty to heads of State and others, when they were 'acts of terrorism' within its Article 1, as read in the scanned copy (LON-1937, item record LON-1937-LOC). CTA6 does not choose between them.

Citations:

- [UNSC1566](../sources/regions/global-un.md#UNSC1566) ([https://undocs.org/S/RES/1566\(2004\)](https://undocs.org/S/RES/1566(2004)))
- [LON-1937-LOC](../sources/regions/europe.md#LON-1937-LOC) ([https://www.loc.gov/item/2021667893/](https://www.loc.gov/item/2021667893/))

<a id="T080"></a>
## T080

- Date: 2004-12-16
- Place: London, United Kingdom
- Region: Europe
- Theme: laws and treaties
- Status: `people-disagree`

Positions differed on Part 4 detention powers: the UK government had enacted them in the 2001 Act, and the House of Lords in A v Secretary of State held the related provision incompatible with the European Convention on Human Rights.

Summary: This row records two positions on the UK's Part 4 detention powers. The UK government had enacted powers in the Anti-terrorism, Crime and Security Act 2001 to detain non-national terrorism suspects (UK-ATCSA2001). On 16 December 2004, the House of Lords in A v Secretary of State for the Home Department declared the related provision (section 23) incompatible with the European Convention on Human Rights (UK-AvSSHD2004). The 2005 control-order Act followed (T082).

Citations:

- Place: Washington, D.C., United States
- Region: North America
- Theme: laws and treaties
- Status: `we-have-a-record`

The Intelligence Reform and Terrorism Prevention Act of 2004 was enacted.

Summary: On 17 December 2004, the Intelligence Reform and Terrorism Prevention Act of 2004 was enacted. Its long title says it reforms the US intelligence community and the Government's intelligence activities. It came five months after the 9/11 Commission Report (T077).

Citation: [US-IRTPA2004](../sources/regions/north-america.md#US-IRTPA2004) ([https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/PLAW-108publ458/pdf/PLAW-108publ458.pdf](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/PLAW-108publ458/pdf/PLAW-108publ458.pdf))

- Date: 2005-03-11
- Place: London, United Kingdom
- Region: Europe
- Theme: laws and treaties
- Status: `we-have-a-record`

The UK Parliament enacted the Prevention of Terrorism Act 2005 (control orders).

Summary: On 11 March 2005, the UK Parliament enacted the Prevention of Terrorism Act 2005, which created control orders. It followed the House of Lords ruling on Part 4 detention (T080). Control orders were abolished and replaced by TPIMs in 2011 (T106).

Citation: [UK-PTA2005](../sources/regions/europe.md#UK-PTA2005) ([https://www.legislation.gov.uk/ukpga/2005/2/contents](https://www.legislation.gov.uk/ukpga/2005/2/contents))

- Place: New York, United States (UN General Assembly)
- Region: Global/UN
- Theme: laws and treaties
- Status: `we-have-a-record`

The International Convention for the Suppression of Acts of Nuclear Terrorism was adopted.

Summary: On 13 April 2005, the UN General Assembly adopted the International Convention for the Suppression of Acts of Nuclear Terrorism. According to the UN Office of Counter-Terrorism, it covers acts against targets including nuclear power plants and reactors, as well as threats and attempts, and requires offenders to be extradited or prosecuted.

Citations:

- [CONV-NUCLEAR2005](../sources/regions/global-un.md#CONV-NUCLEAR2005) ([https://treaties.un.org/doc/db/Terrorism/english-18-15.pdf](https://treaties.un.org/doc/db/Terrorism/english-18-15.pdf))

- Date: 2005-04-21

- Region: Global/UN
- Theme: UN and international frameworks
- Status: `not-proven`

The UN Commission on Human Rights adopted resolution 2005/80, creating a Special Rapporteur on human rights while countering terrorism (source text not machine-verified).

Summary: This milestone is not proven. The OHCHR page on the Special Rapporteur states that in April 2005 the Commission on Human Rights created the mandate through resolution 2005/80, and that part is backed. According to an unofficial copy of the resolution (SEC-CHR-2005-80-SCR), it was adopted without a vote on 21 April 2005 and paragraph 14 appointed the special rapporteur for three years. The official resolution text could not be retrieved from the UN document system, so its adoption and contents are not machine-verified; confidence stays not-proven.

Citations:

The Council of Europe Convention on the Prevention of Terrorism (CETS No. 196) was opened for signature.

Summary: This milestone is not proven. The Council of Europe Convention on the Prevention of Terrorism (CETS No. 196) is recorded as opened for signature on 16 May 2005 in Warsaw. The official treaty text, now the cited copy, supports the date and place ('Done at Warsaw, this 16th day of May 2005'); an explanatory report that uses the words 'opened for signature' has been identified but not yet read.

- Notes: An explanatory report has been identified but not yet read. The official treaty text supports the date and place; the words 'opened for signature' have not been confirmed from a fetched page, so this row stays not-proven.

- Region: Europe
- Theme: UN and international frameworks
- Status: `we-have-a-record`

Bombs exploded on London's transport system; the UN Security Council adopted resolution 1611 (2005) the same day.

Summary: On 7 July 2005, bombs exploded on London's transport system, and the UN Security Council adopted resolution 1611 the same day, condemning the attacks without reservation. The UK Home Office published an official account in 2006, and the Intelligence and Security Committee later reviewed the intelligence (T100).

- Region: Global/UN
- Theme: UN and international frameworks
- Status: `we-have-a-record`

The UN Security Council adopted resolution 1624 (2005) on incitement to commit terrorist acts.

Summary: On 14 September 2005, the UN Security Council adopted resolution 1624 on incitement to commit terrorist acts. It calls on all States to prohibit incitement by law in line with international law, to strengthen border security, and to promote dialogue among civilizations.

Citation: [UNSC1624](../sources/regions/global-un.md#UNSC1624) ([https://undocs.org/S/RES/1624\(2005\)](https://undocs.org/S/RES/1624(2005)))

Summary: On 30 November 2005, the EU Presidency and the EU Counter-Terrorism Co-ordinator forwarded the European Union Counter-Terrorism Strategy (Council document 14469/4/05 REV 4) to the Council for agreement, for onward transmission to the European Council. The document backs the date, place and document number; the date of formal adoption is not stated in it \[UNKNOWN\]. It is the EU's overall counter-terrorism strategy.

- Place: London, United Kingdom
- Region: Europe
- Theme: laws and treaties
- Status: `we-have-a-record`

The UK Parliament enacted the Terrorism Act 2006.

Summary: On 30 March 2006, the UK Parliament enacted the Terrorism Act 2006. It created offences including encouragement of terrorism, dissemination of terrorist publications, preparation of terrorist acts and terrorist training.

Citation: [UK-TA2006](../sources/regions/europe.md#UK-TA2006) ([https://www.legislation.gov.uk/ukpga/2006/11/contents](https://www.legislation.gov.uk/ukpga/2006/11/contents))

- Status: `people-disagree`

Positions differed on military commissions: the 2001 Military Order created them, and the US Supreme Court in H. v. Rumsfeld, 548 U.S. 557 (2006), held that the military commission convened to try the petitioner lacked power to proceed.

Summary: This row records two positions on military commissions. The President's Military Order of 13 November 2001 created them (US-MILORDER2001). On 29 June 2006, the US Supreme Court in H. v. Rumsfeld, 548 U.S. 557, held that the commission convened to try the petitioner lacked power to proceed because its structure and procedures violated the Uniform Code of Military Justice and the Geneva Conventions (USSC-2006-548-557). Congress passed the Military Commissions Act later that year (T092).

Citations:

- [USSC-2006-548-557](../sources/regions/north-america.md#USSC-2006-548-557) ([https://tile.loc.gov/storage-services/service/ll/usrep/usrep548/usrep548557/usrep548557.pdf](https://tile.loc.gov/storage-services/service/ll/usrep/usrep548/usrep548557/usrep548557.pdf))

- Theme: UN and international frameworks

The UN General Assembly adopted the United Nations Global Counter-Terrorism Strategy (A/RES/60/288).

Summary: On 8 September 2006, the UN General Assembly adopted the United Nations Global Counter-Terrorism Strategy (A/RES/60/288), with a plan of action annexed. The UN Office of Counter-Terrorism describes it as adopted by consensus. In 2017 the Assembly created an office to help States implement it (T121).

Citation: [UNGA60-288](../sources/regions/global-un.md#UNGA60-288) ([https://undocs.org/A/RES/60/288](https://undocs.org/A/RES/60/288))

- Region: North America
- Theme: laws and treaties
- Status: `we-have-a-record`

The Military Commissions Act of 2006 was enacted.

Summary: On 17 October 2006, the Military Commissions Act of 2006 was enacted. It authorizes trial by military commission of alien unlawful enemy combatants for violations of the law of war, and it restricted habeas corpus, a point later decided by the Supreme Court (T096). It followed the 2006 Supreme Court ruling recorded at T090.

Citation: [US-MCA2006](../sources/regions/north-america.md#US-MCA2006) ([https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/PLAW-109publ366/pdf/PLAW-109publ366.pdf](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/PLAW-109publ366/pdf/PLAW-109publ366.pdf))

ASEAN member states concluded the ASEAN Convention on Counter Terrorism.

Summary: On 13 January 2007, in Cebu, ASEAN member states concluded the ASEAN Convention on Counter Terrorism. Article I says it provides the framework for regional cooperation to counter, prevent and suppress terrorism.

Summary: In March 2007, the US Justice Department's Office of the Inspector General issued its review of the FBI's use of National Security Letters, as directed by the 2005 PATRIOT Act reauthorization. The UN Security Council adopted resolution 1757 (2007) concerning the Special Tribunal for Lebanon.

Summary: On 30 May 2007, the UN Security Council adopted resolution 1757 concerning the Special Tribunal for Lebanon. Acting under Chapter VII, the Council decided that the provisions establishing the Tribunal would enter into force. It followed the investigation commission created by resolution 1595 in 2005.

Positions differed on habeas corpus for Guantanamo detainees: the Military Commissions Act of 2006 restricted it, and the US Supreme Court in B. v. Bush, 553 U.S. 723 (2008), held detainees have the constitutional privilege of habeas corpus.

Summary: This row records two positions on habeas corpus for Guantanamo detainees. The Military Commissions Act of 2006 restricted it (US-MCA2006). On 12 June 2008, the US Supreme Court in B. v. Bush, 553 U.S. 723, held that the detainees have the constitutional privilege of habeas corpus and are not barred from it by their enemy-combatant designation or their presence at Guantanamo (USSC-2008-553-723).

Citations:

- [USSC-2008-553-723](../sources/regions/north-america.md#USSC-2008-553-723) ([https://tile.loc.gov/storage-services/service/ll/usrep/usrep553/usrep553723/usrep553723.pdf](https://tile.loc.gov/storage-services/service/ll/usrep/usrep553/usrep553723/usrep553723.pdf))

## T097

- Date: 2008-09-03
- Place: Luxembourg (Court of Justice)
- Region: Europe
- Theme: laws and treaties
- Status: `people-disagree`

Positions differed on implementing UN sanctions listings: the Court of Justice in K. and Al Barakaat (Joined Cases C-402/05 P and C-415/05 P) annulled the EU regulation as it concerned the applicants, on fundamental-rights grounds, while the UN 1267 listing regime continued.

Summary: This row records two positions on UN sanctions listings. On 3 September 2008, the EU Court of Justice in K. and Al Barakaat (Joined Cases C-402/05 P and C-415/05 P) annulled the EU regulation implementing the listings as it concerned the applicants, on fundamental-rights grounds (CJEU-2008-C402-05P). The UN 1267 listing regime itself continued (UNSC1267). The UN later created an Ombudsperson for delisting requests (T101).

Citations:

- [CJEU-2008-C402-05P](../sources/regions/europe.md#CJEU-2008-C402-05P) ([https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX:62005CJ0402](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX:62005CJ0402))

- Place: Washington, D.C., United States
- Region: North America
- Theme: laws and treaties
- Status: `we-have-a-record`

Executive Order 13491 on ensuring lawful interrogations was issued.

Summary: On 22 January 2009, US Executive Order 13491, 'Ensuring Lawful Interrogations', was issued. The order says it aims to improve intelligence-gathering, promote the safe, lawful and humane treatment of people in US custody, and ensure compliance with US treaty obligations.

Citation: [US-EO13491](../sources/regions/north-america.md#US-EO13491) ([https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2009/01/27/E9-1885/ensuring-lawful-interrogations](https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2009/01/27/E9-1885/ensuring-lawful-interrogations))

- Region: Europe
- Theme: laws and treaties
- Status: `we-have-a-record`

The ECtHR Grand Chamber delivered judgment in A. and Others v. the United Kingdom on detention under the 2001 Act.

Summary: On 19 February 2009, the Grand Chamber of the European Court of Human Rights delivered judgment in A. and Others v. the United Kingdom on detention under the 2001 Act. According to the Court's factsheet, it found violations of Article 5 § 1 for most applicants because indefinite detention of non-nationals discriminated unjustifiably between nationals and non-nationals, while finding no violation of Article 3. It follows the House of Lords ruling at T080.

Citation: [ECHR-AvUK2009](../sources/regions/europe.md#ECHR-AvUK2009) ([https://hudoc.echr.coe.int/eng?i=001-91403](https://hudoc.echr.coe.int/eng?i=001-91403))

- Region: Europe
- Theme: studies and evaluations
- Status: `we-have-a-record`

The Intelligence and Security Committee published 'Could 7/7 Have Been Prevented?', its review of intelligence on the 7 July 2005 attacks.

Summary: In May 2009, the UK Parliament's Intelligence and Security Committee published 'Could 7/7 Have Been Prevented?', its review of intelligence on the 7 July 2005 attacks (T086). It is a parliamentary oversight review of the work of MI5, MI6 and GCHQ before the attacks; its conclusions are not summarized in CTA6 \[UNKNOWN\].

Citation: [UK-ISC-77-2009](../sources/regions/europe.md#UK-ISC-77-2009) ([https://assets.publishing.service.gov.uk/media/5a7c153540f0b61a825d6582/7-7_attacks_intelligence.pdf](https://assets.publishing.service.gov.uk/media/5a7c153540f0b61a825d6582/7-7_attacks_intelligence.pdf))

- Status: `we-have-a-record`

The UN Security Council adopted resolution 1904 (2009), creating the Office of the Ombudsperson for the Al-Qaida sanctions list.

Summary: On 17 December 2009, the UN Security Council adopted resolution 1904, creating the Office of the Ombudsperson for the Al-Qaida sanctions list. The Ombudsperson handles requests from those seeking removal from the list. The listing process had also been challenged in court (T097).

Citation: [UNSC1904](../sources/regions/global-un.md#UNSC1904) ([https://undocs.org/S/RES/1904\(2009\)](https://undocs.org/S/RES/1904(2009)))

- Region: North America
- Theme: laws and treaties
- Status: `we-have-a-record`

The US Supreme Court decided Holder v. Humanitarian Law Project on the material-support statute.

Summary: On 21 June 2010, the US Supreme Court decided Holder v. Humanitarian Law Project. It held that the federal material-support statute is constitutional as applied to the kinds of support the plaintiffs wanted to give to designated foreign terrorist organizations.

Citation: [US-HLP2010](../sources/regions/north-america.md#US-HLP2010) ([https://tile.loc.gov/storage-services/service/ll/usrep/usrep561/usrep561001/usrep561001.pdf](https://tile.loc.gov/storage-services/service/ll/usrep/usrep561/usrep561001/usrep561001.pdf))

- Theme: studies and evaluations
- Status: `we-have-a-record`

The UN Special Rapporteur on counter-terrorism and human rights issued report A/HRC/16/51 on ten areas of best practices.

Summary: On 22 December 2010, the UN Special Rapporteur on counter-terrorism and human rights, Martin Scheinin, issued report A/HRC/16/51, 'Ten areas of best practices in countering terrorism'. The report says it was his sixth and last annual report to the Human Rights Council and its predecessor. It is an output of the mandate recorded at T084.

The UN Security Council adopted resolutions 1988 (2011) and 1989 (2011), separating the Taliban and Al-Qaida sanctions regimes.

Summary: On 17 June 2011, the UN Security Council adopted resolutions 1988 and 1989, separating the Taliban and Al-Qaida sanctions regimes that had been run together since resolution 1267 (T046). Each regime continued the asset-freeze, travel and arms measures from earlier resolutions.

- [UNSC1989](../sources/regions/global-un.md#UNSC1989) ([https://undocs.org/S/RES/1989\(2011\)](https://undocs.org/S/RES/1989(2011)))

The White House issued the National Strategy for Counterterrorism.

Summary: On 28 June 2011, the White House issued the National Strategy for Counterterrorism. The document says it sets out the overarching goals of US counterterrorism and the steps needed to achieve them.

The UK Parliament enacted the Terrorism Prevention and Investigation Measures Act 2011.

Summary: On 14 December 2011, the UK Parliament enacted the Terrorism Prevention and Investigation Measures Act 2011. It abolished control orders, created under the 2005 Act (T082), and replaced them with TPIMs subject to set conditions, a five-year limit and court scrutiny.

The ECtHR Grand Chamber delivered judgment in E. v. the former Yugoslav Republic of Macedonia (no. 39630/09).

Summary: On 13 December 2012, the Grand Chamber of the European Court of Human Rights delivered judgment in E. v. the former Yugoslav Republic of Macedonia (no. 39630/09). According to the Court's factsheet, it found the State responsible for the applicant's torture and ill-treatment in Skopje and for handing him to CIA agents in a secret 'rendition', a violation of Article 3. It is the first of several rendition judgments in CTA6 (see T110, T168, T181).

- Region: East/Southeast Asia
- Theme: studies and evaluations
- Status: `we-have-a-record`

The National Human Rights Commission of Korea submitted its opinion to the National Assembly in connection with deliberation of the draft Terrorism Prevention Act.

Summary: On 30 November 2001 the National Human Rights Commission of Korea submitted an opinion to the National Assembly on the draft Terrorism Prevention Act then under deliberation, according to its press release of 1 December 2001. The content of the opinion is not recorded in CTA6 \[UNKNOWN\]. It is the first of three Korean oversight records in CTA6, with T232 and T236.

The National Human Rights Commission of Korea announced that its chairperson would deliver the Commission's opposing opinion on the pending draft Terrorism Prevention Act to the Speaker of the National Assembly that afternoon.

Summary: On 4 April 2002 the National Human Rights Commission of Korea posted a notice that its chairperson would visit the National Assembly that afternoon to deliver the Commission's opposing opinion on the pending draft Terrorism Prevention Act. - Place: Pakistan (Parliament)
- Region: South Asia
- Theme: doctrine and strategy
- Status: `we-have-a-record`

According to NACTA, Pakistan's 20-point National Action Plan for countering terrorism and extremism was approved on 24 December 2014 by a special session of Parliament.

Summary: According to Pakistan's National Counter Terrorism Authority, the 20-point National Action Plan was approved by a special session of Parliament on 24 December 2014, after the 16 December 2014 attack on the Army Public School. NACTA states that it was later made the plan's monitoring body. The record comes from an undated NACTA page; the plan document itself is not in CTA6 \[UNKNOWN\].
